Privacy-focused search engine company DuckDuckGo has released a new survey revealing how much personal information users share with AI chatbots, and how little most people understand about where these conversations go. Here are the details.

The survey shows AI users share more data than they realise

In a survey released today, DuckDuckGo highlighted multiple privacy concerns related to people's use of AI chatbots, including that nearly one-third of users have told AI things they wouldn't share with friends, family, colleagues or medical professionals. Among self-identified AI enthusiasts, this figure rises to 56%.

DuckDuckGo stated:

The company noted that of approximately 2,000 American adults surveyed, 53% did not know or were unsure that most chatbots use conversations by default to train models, while only 25% knew that law enforcement agencies can obtain AI conversation records through court subpoenas.

The results also showed significant behavioural differences between parents and non-parents, with parents or guardians of children confiding in AI at nearly twice the rate of non-parents. DuckDuckGo stated: "Among parents using AI, 43% have told AI things they have never told anyone," while "the proportion of AI users without children at home drops to 25%."

DuckDuckGo believes that AI companies have exacerbated this behaviour by encouraging users through advertising campaigns and media appearances to view chatbots as confidants, despite the fact that the privacy of these conversations may not be what users assume.

In terms of trust, the survey found that people have slightly more confidence in large AI companies than in the US government to protect their data. However, both face significant scepticism: 39% said they have no trust at all in large AI companies, while the figure for the government is 48%.

Ultimately, DuckDuckGo believes users still have an opportunity to change how they handle AI privacy, especially while chatbot usage habits are still in an early stage of development:

When we talk about online privacy with search engines and browsers, many people think 'it's too late, my data is already out there.' But the most valuable information you can share with big tech companies is actually your next question, not the questions you asked days, months or years ago. Therefore, it is never too late to switch to more privacy-conscious online services.

The company also reminded users that they can take proactive steps to protect their privacy when using AI chatbots, including choosing services with clearer and more transparent data handling policies.
